summary:
Gentius ruled the Illyrian kingdom from 181 to 168 BC and was its last attested king. Son of Pleuratus III, who had maintained friendly relations with Rome, he initially allied with Rome against Macedon in 171 BC. In 169, he switched sides to support Perseus of Macedon, built up his fleet and army, and arrested Roman envoys. His forces attacked Roman-aligned cities, including Bassania.

In 168 BC, Roman forces under Lucius Anicius Gallus defeated Gentius at Scodra in a campaign lasting about 30 days. Gentius surrendered and was taken to Rome in 167 BC for Anicius’s triumph, then held at Iguvium. Rome divided the conquered territory into three administrative units. Local communities retained elected officials and autonomy, but paid Rome half the taxes they had previously paid Gentius.
unsupportedClaims: The sentence beginning “In 169” dates the fleet and army buildup to that year, but the points do not establish that date.
The sentence beginning “In 169” also dates the arrest of the Roman envoys to that year, but the points place the arrests after Rome invaded Macedonia in 168 BC.

The summary generalizes elected offices, local autonomy, and half-rate taxes to local communities across the conquered territory. The points attribute continued elections and half-rate taxes to spared communities, and local autonomy to the separate koina.
